subject: Business
title: Research: Know More Than the Other Side
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Research: Know More Than the Other Side.

hook.text: A job candidate researched the company's funding round. She knew they'd just raised $50M. She asked for more.

buildup.text: Preparation is the most underused advantage in negotiation. Most people wing it.

discovery.text: Research the other side's constraints, alternatives, deadlines, and decision-makers before you sit down.

twist.text: Information asymmetry is power. The side that knows more about the other's situation almost always wins.

climax.text: Chris Voss says the best FBI negotiators spend 80% of their time preparing and 20% talking.

punchline.text: The negotiation is won before it starts.

quiz.question: Why is preparation the biggest advantage in negotiation?
options: Information asymmetry gives the better-informed side leverage
It shows respect to the other party

details.summary: Preparation is the most reliable predictor of negotiation success. Researching the other side's constraints, alternatives, priorities, and decision-making process gives you informational advantages that improve every aspect of the negotiation from opening offers to creative solutions.
details.whyItMatters: Information is power in negotiation. The party with better information about the other side's situation, alternatives, and constraints can make more precise offers, identify better trades, and avoid leaving value on the table through ignorance.
takeaways: Preparation is the strongest predictor of negotiation outcomes across all studies
Research the other side's constraints, BATNA, and decision-making process thoroughly
Information asymmetry creates negotiation power that tactics alone cannot match

faq.question: What specific information should you research before a negotiation?
faq.answer: The other side's alternatives and BATNA. Their decision-making authority and process. Their time constraints and deadlines. Their past negotiation patterns. Market benchmarks for the issues being discussed. Their organizational priorities and pressures. Their reputation and style.

faq.question: How much time should you spend preparing versus negotiating?
faq.answer: Expert negotiators recommend spending at least as much time preparing as you expect to spend at the table. For high-stakes negotiations, the ratio should be even higher. Most negotiators under-prepare and attempt to compensate with improvisation, which is far less effective.
